analysis.one_liner: Restores 2009-level estate and gift taxes and directs that revenue into Social Security.
analysis.headline: A one-sponsor Senate bill to raise estate and gift taxes to 2009 levels and steer that revenue to Social Security has sat without cosponsors or committee action since its introduction in March 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bring back the estate and gift tax rules in effect in 2009: estates above $3.5 million would again face taxes climbing to a 45 percent top rate, and large lifetime gifts would be taxed at that level too. It would also merge the two Social Security trust funds into one and direct all estate and gift tax revenue into that fund, adding a new revenue stream for benefits beyond payroll taxes. The bill was introduced by a single senator, referred to the Finance Committee, and has moved no further.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security's roughly 70 million beneficiaries and future retirees, since the added revenue would extend the program's solvency without raising payroll taxes on workers or cutting benefits. Workers also benefit indirectly because the bill funds the program with a tax on inherited wealth rather than wages.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: The bill restores the 2009 estate tax rate schedule, under which taxable estates over $1.5 million face rates rising to 45 percent, and cuts the exempted amount per person from current law to $3.5 million.

It applies the same 45 percent structure to large gifts, and limits the tax-free amount a surviving spouse can inherit from the first spouse's unused exemption, closing a common way couples shelter large estates.

The bill combines the Old-Age and Survivors and Disability trust funds into a single Social Security Trust Fund and amends the Social Security Act so that 100 percent of estate and gift tax revenue is appropriated into it each year, alongside payroll tax revenue.
The revenue would begin flowing for fiscal years after January 1, 2027, with the tax changes applying to people who die or make gifts after December 31, 2026.

analysis.who_pays: The wealthiest households. Only estates and gifts above roughly $3.5 million per person would face the higher tax, and the 45 percent rate applies at the top. Heirs of very large estates would receive smaller inheritances, and wealthy families would face higher costs to plan around the tax.

drawbacks.text: Opponents of higher estate taxes argue the tax double-taxes wealth that was already taxed when earned, and can force family businesses or farms to sell assets to pay the bill, though the $3.5 million per-person exemption shields the vast majority of farms and small businesses from any tax at all.

The bill redirects a source of general federal revenue to Social Security, meaning the estate and gift tax would no longer help pay for other federal spending or deficit reduction; Congress would have to make that up elsewhere.

Raising the rate back to 45 percent creates strong incentives for wealthy families to use avoidance strategies and for estate planning professionals to market them, so the actual revenue collected may fall short of what the statutory rates suggest.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost falls narrowly on the richest few thousand estates a year, while the benefit — a new dedicated revenue stream for a program nearly every retiree depends on — is broad. The main honest concerns are the general-revenue tradeoff and tax avoidance, not the burden on ordinary families, who are untouched by the $3.5 million exemption.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate, read twice, and sent to the Finance Committee, where it has received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Chris Van Hollen introduced the Strengthen Social Security by Taxing Dynastic Wealth Act in the Senate on March 25, 2026.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance; the committee has taken no further action on it.
No other senator has cosponsored the bill.
The bill text would restore the 2009 estate and gift tax structure and direct all estate and gift tax revenue into a merged Social Security Trust Fund starting January 1, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: the wealthiest estates continue to be taxed under current law's more generous rules, and Social Security receives no new revenue from inherited wealth. The Finance Committee's inaction preserves the status quo for wealthy households.

for.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee; the sole sponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 25, 2026 and has scheduled no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill.

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: As chair, controls the committee's agenda and has not brought the bill up for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and the bill has no cosponsors of either party, so the partisan shape cannot be measured; a single Democratic sponsor faces a Republican-controlled committee agenda.

industries.note: Estates above $3.5 million per person would again face rates up to 45 percent, and the bill's title targets dynastic wealth specifically. Fewer than 0.2 percent of estates currently pay any estate tax, so the cost is concentrated at the very top while the revenue is shared broadly through Social Security.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth management services
industries.note: Higher estate and gift tax rates and a lower exemption increase the value of lawyers, trust planners, and advisors who specialize in minimizing transfer taxes — and equally shrink that market. Ordinary families rarely use these services at this scale.

These businesses are the standard argument against higher estate taxes, but the $3.5 million per-person exemption (up to $7 million for a married couple) means only the largest estates would owe anything. Most would be unaffected.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no committee action five months before the next Congress ends, the bill almost certainly dies in the Finance Committee. Estate tax increases have repeatedly failed to advance even with more cosponsors, and the bill would need to clear both a Senate committee and floor, plus the House, by January 2027.
